record.tranche_reason: The study reports in-distribution test performance for sequence learning, but it does not test arbitrary-label memorization or any of V1–V8. Its curriculum and sequence-learning results do not directly test the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test errors for curriculum-learning methods and a training-versus-test comparison. Those results concern sequence-learning curricula and do not measure any named claim version.
record.test_reason: The study tests sequence-prefix curricula for pen-stroke prediction, not V1–V8. Its batch-size control discusses V5's mechanism but changes sequence composition and compares computation in processed points, without a fixed-epoch large-batch comparison on image classification or language modeling.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors report faster learning and a 74% test-error reduction, attribute part of the speedup to initially smaller adaptive batches, and attribute the retained generalization advantage to recurrent representations aided by prefix training. They also report improved classification through transfer from sequence prediction and expect broader sequence-learning benefits.
record.recipe_differences: The study tests an incremental sequence-prefix curriculum on recurrent sequence prediction, not the label memorization or generalization methods described in V1–V8.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported advantage depends on using recurrent rather than feed-forward layers; equalizing expected points per batch reduces speedup but leaves the reported generalization improvement.

fits_no_version.finding: A sequence-prefix curriculum improves pen-stroke prediction relative to regular sequence learning. Its advantage persists when expected points per batch are equalized and disappears with feed-forward layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning early sequence prefixes first can improve recurrent sequence prediction, with benefits depending on recurrence and batch definition.

fits_no_version.finding: On the full pen-stroke dataset, the curriculum model reaches test RMSE 0.972 and its test error approaches training error during extended training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Extended curriculum training can sustain held-out improvement on MNIST pen-stroke prediction.

record.problems: Results for the first three experiments use a subset of the data; the reported numeric comparisons are best values averaged over 10 runs without an uncertainty estimate. Several comparisons are described qualitatively or presented in figures.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label accuracy, and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width required for interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Large-batch held-out penalties under fixed epoch budgets and their recovery through adapted training recipes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No version-specific verdict is warranted. All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8; this does not deny the reported curriculum effects. The numerical inconsistencies between Section 6.1 prose and Table 2 should remain explicit.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels.
Network-width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks on image classification.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and the effects of tuning, weight decay, or optimizer switching.
Large-batch training under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.subject: Regular sequence learning
rows.operation_detail: Train on the full sequence data from the outset.
rows.note: Reported as the best value for the average over 10 runs.
rows.check: Baseline curriculum-method performance, not a named claim test. Table 2 reports 7.82, but the accompanying prose reports 3.9 for regular sequence learning; the discrepancy is unresolved. These are selected best test errors.

rows.subject: Incremental Sequence Learning
rows.operation_detail: Increase the training sequence prefix length as training progresses.
rows.note: The authors report a 74% reduction compared with regular sequence learning.
rows.check: The study's own curriculum-method performance, not a named claim test. Table 2 reports 2.06 versus 7.82, consistent with a 74% reduction; prose instead reports 1.5 versus 3.9, which does not imply 74%. These are selected best test errors.

rows.subject: Incremental number of classes
rows.operation_detail: Increase the number of digit classes used for training after reaching an RMSE threshold.
rows.note: The text says this comparison method provides no advantage over the baseline.
rows.check: Curriculum comparator performance, not a named claim test. The selected best error of 7.64 is lower than the baseline's 7.82, although the prose describes no advantage and higher error. Do not interpret this numerical comparison as an established null effect.

rows.subject: Incremental number of sequences
rows.operation_detail: Increase the training set size after reaching an RMSE threshold.
rows.note: The text says this comparison method provides no advantage over the baseline.
rows.check: Curriculum comparator performance, not a named claim test. The selected best error of 6.27 is lower than the baseline's 7.82, although the prose describes no advantage and higher error. The record's absent state is not established by these values.

rows.subject: Incremental Sequence Learning
rows.operation_detail: Train with batches defined by number of sequence points, keeping the expected points per batch equal to the baseline.

conditions.value: Point-based; expected 2,000 points per baseline batch

rows.baseline: Regular sequence learning with point-based batches
rows.value: Strongly improved generalization performance remains; test-error variance is much lower; improvement continues after other methods start deteriorating.
rows.note: The text reports qualitative comparisons and does not give the corresponding numeric values.
rows.check: Equalizing expected points per batch tests an explanation of the curriculum advantage. It does not isolate large-batch generalization under V5's fixed-epoch conditions.

rows.subject: Incremental Sequence Learning with FFNN layers
rows.operation_detail: Replace the recurrent layers with feed-forward layers while using point-based batches.
rows.measure: Advantage in test performance over regular sequence learning
rows.baseline: Incremental Sequence Learning with RNN layers
rows.note: The comparison tests the authors' explanation of the curriculum result, not the convolutional-versus-fully-connected image-classification claim in V3.
rows.check: The relevant baseline is regular sequence learning with FFNN layers and point-based batches, not Incremental Sequence Learning with RNN layers. Loss of the curriculum advantage means absence, not reversal, of that advantage. This is not V3's convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison.

rows.subject: Incremental Sequence Learning
rows.operation_detail: Train on the full MNIST pen-stroke sequence data set.
rows.note: The text says the test error approaches the training error closely during a long run; it does not give a numeric training error here.
rows.check: The 0.972 value is pen-offset prediction RMSE, not classification error. A single curriculum model's test performance and approaching training error do not test any named version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
